SOURCE: An Introduction to Vision-Language Modeling, Bordes, Pang, Ajay, Li, Bardes, et al. (Meta and academic co-authors), preprint, arXiv:2405.17247v1, 2024.

COVERAGE: 223,824 of 223,824 chars read, pp. 1-76. References (pp. 48-76) were skimmed for origins. PDF page equals printed page. I checked the numeric quotes by string match against the extraction, with whitespace normalised and line-end hyphens rejoined.

The authors say the work "should not be considered as a survey or a complete guide on VLMs" (p4). Nearly every number is reported second-hand from a cited paper, so cite the primary for any number you use.

CLAIMS

**What trains, by family**

- claim: MiniGPT-4 trains only a linear projection between a pretrained visual encoder and Vicuna, in two rounds.
  number: 20k steps, batch 256, ~5M pairs; 4 A100s, ~10 hours; then 400 steps, batch 12
  setup: BLIP-2 visual encoder; Conceptual Captions, SBU and LAION, then curated instruction data
  quote: "requires only training the linear project layer which is done in two rounds. The first involves 20k training steps (with a batch size of 256), corresponding to around 5M image-text pairs"; "only used four A100 GPUs for around ten hours"; "needing only 400 training steps (with a batch size of 12)"
  where: p15, §2.5.2
- claim: LLaVA 1.5 is cheap to train by instruction tuning. The paper does not say which parts are frozen.
  number: 600k pairs; ~1 day on 8 A100s
  setup: MLP projector plus academic VQA instruction data
  quote: "LLava 1.5 is trained on 600k image-text pairs"; "Training takes approximately one day on 8-A100 GPUs."
  where: p27, §3.5.1
- claim: Frozen keeps the language model frozen and trains the vision encoder and linear map from scratch, and the authors call the freeze crucial. Performance was modest.
  number: 7B-parameter language model
  setup: NF-ResNet-50; text generation objective on Conceptual Captions
  quote: "a 7 billion-parameter transformer trained on C4 [Raffel et al., 2020]) is kept frozen (this is crucial to maintain the features that the pre-trained model had already learned)"
  where: p15, §2.5.1
- claim: BLIP-2 freezes both pretrained models and trains only the Q-Former mapper.
  number: ~100-200M trainable parameters
  setup: CLIP-style encoder, OPT-style LLM
  quote: "A relatively small (∼100-200M parameters) component called a Q-Former is trained for this mapping"
  where: p16, §2.5.3
- claim: Using a pretrained LLM saves compute, but the VLM inherits its defects, and correcting them can add overhead.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement, not a measurement
  quote: "the VLM will be impacted by the potential hallucination of the LLM. It could also be impacted by any bias coming from the pretrained models."
  where: p24, §3.3.4
- claim: Monkey keeps the encoder static, adds LoRA and a trainable resampler, and tiles the image with a sliding window to raise resolution.
  number: up to 1344×896, against a typical 224×224 (the 224 figure has dated)
  setup: scene-text VQA, document VQA, key information extraction
  quote: "enhanced with LoRA adjustments and a trainable visual resampler"; "up to 1344×896 pixels"; "limited to a resolution of 224 x 224"
  where: p28, §3.6

**Parameter-efficient fine-tuning**

- claim: Full fine-tuning becomes impractical as models grow. PEFT methods fall into four groups: LoRA, prompt, adapter and mapping.
  number: none
  setup: taxonomy
  quote: "fine-tuning the entire parameter set of these models becomes impractical due to computational constraints"
  where: p29, §3.7
- claim: QLoRA backpropagates through a frozen quantized model into the LoRA weights.
  number: 4-bit
  setup: pure language model context as described; no memory figure given
  quote: "through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pre-trained language model into LoRA"
  where: p29
- claim: VPT adds trainable inputs while the backbone stays frozen, with accuracy comparable or better "in many instances".
  number: <1% of parameters
  setup: large vision Transformers, not VLMs specifically
  quote: "VPT introduces a minimal amount (less than 1% of model parameters) of trainable parameters in the input space."
  where: p30
- claim: Adapters with weight-sharing can rival full fine-tuning.
  number: 4.18% and 3.39% of parameters updated
  setup: VL-adapter; unified multi-task image-text and video-text benchmarks
  quote: "(4.18% for image-text tasks and 3.39% for video-text tasks)"
  where: p30
- claim: Mapping-based methods keep both modules frozen and need fewer parameters and less data. A per-feature linear map raises sequence length and cost, which MAPL addresses by aggregating into learnable query tokens.
  number: none
  setup: LiMBeR versus MAPL
  quote: "the length of the sequence passed to the LLM is the same as the number of visual feature vectors, increasing the computational cost of training and inference"
  where: pp30-31

**Training data**

- claim: Instruction-tuning sets are far smaller than pretraining sets, but the examples the paper gives are not all in the stated range.
  number: "a few to one hundred thousand" (the unit after "few" is ambiguous); LLaVA 150k; MIMIC-IT ~2.8M
  setup: LLaVA and Otter
  quote: "data sizes ranging from a few to one hundred thousand samples"; "generate 150k synthetically generated visual instruction samples"; "around 2.8M multimodal instruction-response pairs"
  where: pp26-27
- claim: Fine-grained human annotation is costly and scarce, so it suits evaluation or fine-tuning rather than pretraining.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement; many such datasets rely on COCO or Visual Genome imagery
  quote: "more suited for evaluation or fine-tuning than for large-scale pre-training"
  where: p21, §3.1.5
- claim: Adding text-rich instruction data improved a LLaVA model on text VQA, with only a slight gain on natural images.
  number: 422K images, 16K conversations, up to 20%
  setup: LLaVAR; OCR output plus captions fed to text-only GPT-4
  quote: "422K text-rich images"; "generate 16K conversations"; "with up to a 20% accuracy improvement on text-based VQA datasets"
  where: p28, §3.6
- claim: Performance tracks how often a concept appears in training, and this can be estimated before training by running a recognition model over the data.
  number: none
  setup: Udandarao et al. 2024; RAM as the recognition model
  quote: "zero-shot performances of VLMs depend mostly on how much those zero-shot downstream concepts are present in the training data"
  where: p19, p40 §4.2.4
- claim: Deduplicate and prune the data, since duplicates waste compute and risk memorization.
  number: none
  setup: Figure 2 caption
  quote: "It is also important to remove duplicates which occur a lot within large-scale datasets, this will save a lot of compute time and mitigate the risks of memorization."
  where: p17
- claim: Labels generated by a model inherit its errors. Synthetic caption gains also cap at scale.
  number: none
  setup: Kosmos-2 with GLIP; Nguyen et al. 2023
  quote: "It is likely that if this base model fails on some rare nouns or instances, the downstream model would make similar mistakes."; "the improvement provided by synthetic captions is capped by the limited diversity of generated captions"
  where: p25, p19

**Compute**

- claim: From-scratch training is the expensive path. The 64-GPU figure is the authors' estimate, not a reported run.
  number: hundreds to thousands of GPUs; OpenCLIP 256-600; estimate ≤64 GPUs, ~10K USD
  setup: 64 GPUs assumes a contrastive model on hundreds of millions of images, a high-quality dataset, and masking on bigger models
  quote: "hundreds to thousands of GPUs while having to use hundreds of millions of images and text pairs"; "between 256 and 600 GPUs across multiple days or weeks depending on the model size"; "should not require more than 64 GPUs (which should be equivalent to spending around 10K USD in compute)"
  where: p14, p16, p22
- claim: Data loading is an overlooked bottleneck. Random masking of image tokens speeds training.
  number: none
  setup: torch.compile, xformers, FFCV; Li et al. 2023f for masking
  quote: "The main recommendation we have is to store as many uncompressed files as possible"; "randomly masking image tokens one can significantly speed up training time while improving model performances"
  where: p22
- claim: Resolution, encoder capacity and visual pretraining data matter most, and how the modalities are connected matters much less.
  number: none
  setup: McKinzie et al. 2024 (MM1), secondary report; measured on zero-shot classification and VQA
  quote: "image resolution, visual encoder capacity, and visual pretraining data are the choices that most impact model performance"
  where: p23

**Evaluation and failure modes**

- claim: A tie between captions can score perfectly in binary-caption benchmarks, because argmax returns the first element and the correct caption is often placed first. The authors recommend adding a small random epsilon or tracking ties.
  number: 100%
  setup: benchmarks that discriminate a correct caption from a negative one
  quote: "a model whose parameters are all equal to zero could achieve 100% accuracy in these benchmarks"
  where: p37, §4.1.6
- claim: Benchmarks can be solved from language alone. Winoground and EqBen penalize these shortcuts, while ARO, Crepe, VL-CheckList and SugarCrepe are susceptible.
  number: 98%
  setup: original VQA; Lin et al. 2024a for the blind language prior
  quote: "has the answer “yes”98% of the time"
  where: p40, §4.2.3
- claim: VQA Accuracy is too strict for free-form generators, and formatting tricks distort comparison. Mañas et al. 2024 propose LLMs as judges.
  number: none
  setup: generative models, OOD evaluation
  quote: "too stringent and tends to underestimate the performance of current VLM systems"
  where: p34, §4.1.3
- claim: Selective prediction measures whether a model abstains instead of answering wrongly, which suits accuracy-critical uses.
  number: none
  setup: Whitehead et al. 2022; Effective Reliability is the cost-based metric
  quote: "defining evaluation in terms of coverage (the fraction of questions answered) at a specified risk"
  where: p34
- claim: Scarce instruction data can misalign the modalities and cause hallucination. Factually Augmented RLHF is reported to reduce this.
  number: 94% of GPT-4 on LLaVA-Bench; 60% over baselines on MMHAL-BENCH
  setup: LLaVA-RLHF; baselines and metric not named here
  quote: "may misalign the vision and language modalities and generate hallucinated outputs"; "LLaVA-RLHF achieves 94% performance level of GPT-4 [Achiam et al., 2023]. On MMHAL-BENCH with a special focus on penalizing hallucinations, LLaVA-RLHF outperforms baselines by 60%."
  where: p27
- claim: CHAIR misleads on long generations and is limited to COCO. Alternatives are POPE (binary polling), GAVIE, CCEval and MMHal-Bench (GPT-4 based), and human evaluation.
  number: none
  setup: object hallucination benchmarks
  quote: "it can be misleading for evaluating long generations from recent VLMs"; "which is often included in training sets"
  where: pp40-41, §4.3
- claim: VLMs did no better than chance on spatial relations in a controlled synthetic test.
  number: none (random chance)
  setup: PUG, Bordes et al. 2023; the object is moved left or right within a scene
  quote: "current VLMs are not performing better than random chance when evaluating spatial relations"
  where: p38, §4.1.8
- claim: Randomly masking caption tokens each epoch was the most effective regularizer against memorization, without severely penalizing utility.
  number: none
  setup: Jayaraman et al. 2024, CLIP; k-NN gap between target and reference models
  quote: "text randomization to be the most effective regularization technique"
  where: p41, §4.4
- claim: Measured bias can reflect the evaluation data, through label quality or image sources that vary by group. CLIPScore is limited by the CLIP model behind it. Grounding has no single fix (p25).
  number: none
  setup: Hall et al. 2023a; Scheuerman et al. 2023
  quote: "label quality of evaluation data can vary, with potential bias for certain groups"
  where: p39, p33

LIMITS

What the paper does not say on fine-tuning:
- **Freezing:** there is no procedure for deciding what to freeze when adapting an existing VLM to your own domain. Unfreezing top encoder or LLM layers is not discussed. Its only general rule is that a pretrained backbone suits limited compute (p24), and the only stated reason to freeze is Frozen's (p15).
- **Hyperparameters:** there are no learning rates, epochs, optimizers, LoRA rank or target modules, or per-group learning rates. MiniGPT-4 is the only fine-tuning recipe with step and batch counts.
- **Memory:** there are no VRAM figures, and no mention of gradient checkpointing or mixed precision. Cost of image tokens appears only as LiMBeR's sequence-length remark and MiniGPT4-Video's token merging. Compute is given as GPU counts and hours. The 24× storage/processing figure applies to video (p42).
- **Data:** there is no minimum dataset size for domain fine-tuning, and no guidance on holdouts or train/validation splits.
- **Evaluation during training:** §4 covers benchmarks only. Nothing addresses in-training monitoring, early stopping, overfitting checks, or before-and-after regression testing, apart from memorization tests.
- **Effect of fine-tuning on failures:** LLaVA-RLHF's 60% is the only hallucination gain reported. No figure shows how fine-tuning changes bias.
- **Peft comparisons:** there is no head-to-head of LoRA against adapters or mapping on one VLM task.

What the authors concede:
- It is incomplete by design (p4).
- There is no holistic way to measure multimodal data quality: "we lack a holistic way of evaluating the quality of multimodal and interleaved data" (p21).
- Many benchmarks have "severe limitations" (p46).

What has dated: this is v1 from May 2024. The 224×224 norm, the model lineup and the cloud cost estimate are all from that period.

BUILDS ON: LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023), adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019), VPT (Jia et al., 2022), CoOp (Zhou et al., 2022), VL-adapter (Sung et al., 2022), LLaMA-Adapter V2 (Gao et al., 2023), LiMBeR (Merullo et al., 2022), MAPL (Mañas et al., 2023), Vallaeys et al. (2024), MM1 (McKinzie et al., 2024), Udandarao et al. (2024), LLaVA-RLHF (Sun et al., 2023), POPE (Li et al., 2023g), CHAIR (Rohrbach et al., 2018), Goyal et al. (2017), Lin et al. (2024a), Whitehead et al. (2022), Mañas et al. (2024), DataComp (Gadre et al., 2023), masking (Li et al., 2023f), Jayaraman et al. (2024).

CODE: none in the paper. It only points to OpenCLIP and transformers, and it recommends them for benchmarking and comparing models (p22), not for fine-tuning.

FIGURES
- Figure 2, p17, "Important considerations to keep in mind when training VLMs": one view linking data curation, grounding and alignment, faster than §3's prose.
- Figure 3, p32, "Different methods to evaluate VLMs": shows VQA, reasoning, dense annotation and synthetic evaluation side by side, with example images.
- Figure 1, p7, "Families of VLMs": probably redundant with your existing anatomy section, though it contrasts the four training paradigms.

PROBLEMS
- **Embedded instructions:** none found (keyword scan plus full read).
- **Extraction:** text is clean, with some lost spaces, mostly in reference entries, and glued text such as “yes”98%. Equations are garbled but not needed here. Quotes that cross a line have the line break normalised.
- **Conflict with your note:** this paper gives LLaVA 1.5 "600k image-text pairs" (p27). notes/01-image-input.md line 34 gives "1.2M public training examples", citing arXiv:2310.03744. Check the primary before reusing either figure.
- **Internal inconsistency on MiniGPT-4:** p15 says it trains only the linear layer, while p30 groups it under "other full-fine-tuning approaches like MiniGPT-4 and LLaVA". Do not use p30 as evidence of what LLaVA or MiniGPT-4 freeze.
- **Internal inconsistency on OpenCLIP:** "between 256 and 600 GPUs" (p16) against "more than 500 GPUs" for CLIP and OpenCLIP (p22).
- **Typos in the source:** "LLaVa-RLFH" (p26) and "Attribution" for ARO. The source spells it hallucination throughout, and quotes keep the source spelling.
